source.title: DriveGPT: Scaling Autoregressive Behavior Models for Driving
source.authors: Xin Huang; Eric M. Wolff; P. Vernaza; Tung Phan-Minh; Hongge Chen; David S. Hayden; Mark Edmonds; Brian Pierce; Xin-Xin Chen; Pratik Elias Jacob; Xiao-Bai Chen; Chingiz Tairbekov; Pratik Agarwal; Tianshi Gao; Yuning Chai; Siddhartha S. Srinivasa

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests loss and scaling behavior in an autonomous-driving behavior model, extending scaling-law measurements to a non-text modality and task.
record.gate_note: The paper reports internal validation cross-entropy scaling results and downstream planning and motion-prediction results. It cites language-model scaling studies as motivation, but the cited studies' results are not recorded as rows. Extrapolated sample-count estimates are predictions from the fit, not observations on runs trained with those additional samples.
record.test_reason: Fits held-out next-action cross-entropy against data, model size and compute for an autoregressive transformer driving-behaviour model. This is a new, non-text setting with its own scaling results, bearing mainly on V5 and, in that setting, on V3, V4 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report LLM-like scaling with data and compute, diminishing returns with model size, data as the main bottleneck, and downstream planning and WOMD prediction gains from scale and pretraining. Add that they say driving metrics keep improving past the point where validation loss plateaus.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an autoregressive transformer and cross-entropy loss, and measures loss versus data, parameters, and compute, but applies them to driving states and actions rather than text; model/data/compute sweeps and fitting procedures are specific to the driving setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The model-scaling effect depends on training-data size; performance depends on learning-rate selection; changing attention heads has a smaller effect than hidden dimension overall, and scaling encoder and decoder components separately changes results. Fixed-compute results also show data-bottleneck effects.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal maximum learning rate decreases with model size, from 0.005 at 1.5M to 0.0001 at 1.4B parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal learning rate falls with model size in scaled transformers.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The main loss-scaling results are largely presented in figures, with few numerical loss values stated in text. No uncertainty intervals or statistical tests are reported for the scaling curves. The training dataset is an internal research dataset. Compute-scaling experiments cover only a subset of the FLOP range used in the cited language-model studies.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the paper's extrapolated estimates of 350M additional examples for a 10% best-loss improvement or about 1.4B for a 20% improvement: these are projections from the fitted curve, not observed training outcomes. No further downstream benchmark rows were included because they do not directly test the scaling-law loss or allocation claims.

untested.parts: No language models; no text pretraining loss.
The extrapolations (350M or 1.4B extra samples; 70M or 500M for perplexity targets) are never checked against larger runs.
No fitted parameter or token exponents; no Kaplan vs Hoffmann comparison.
Depth versus width is not varied at fixed parameter count.
No image or video models, repeated data, or fitted fine-tuning/transfer laws.
No comparison of fitting methods, parameter counting or schedules; no comparison with published exponents.

missing.what: Perplexity vs dataset size fit: log P = -0.28 log D + 7.22, R2 0.994
DriveGPT-WOMD model scaling: minFDE 1.4297 at 2M falls to 1.2846 at 14M, with no gain at 21M (1.2871) because of limited data
WOMD test set: DriveGPT-Finetune vs DriveGPT-WOMD, minADE 0.5240 vs 0.5279, MR 0.1202 vs 0.1236

record.verdict_notes: This is a new setting: a driving behaviour model rather than a text LM. Rows on V3, V4 and V6 are linked under T3 as results in that setting. Loss-curve values are mostly figure-only, and no uncertainty is reported beyond R2. The data range is under two orders of magnitude.

versions.untested_parts: No language models or language-model held-out pretraining losses are tested.

The paper extrapolates from its data-scaling fit to estimate additional sample counts for target improvements, but does not compare those predictions with observed losses from runs orders of magnitude larger.

The study examines fixed-compute allocations qualitatively, but does not report fitted parameter-count and token-count exponents or establish a stable power-law allocation. Its resource axes are model parameters and driving-data samples, not language-model tokens.
Tests attention-head and encoder/decoder scaling choices, but does not systematically vary depth and width independently across a wide range at fixed parameter count.
Tests driving behavior models and reports a data-size loss fit, but does not test image or video models, repeated-data training, or a power-law loss fit for fine-tuning or transfer.

Reports downstream driving metrics against data and model scale and reports motion-prediction gains from more pretraining data; it does not fit a relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss.

Shows dependence on data size, architecture choices, and a loss curve that slows or plateaus, but does not compare alternative fitting methods or quantify disagreement between published exponents or compute-optimal allocation laws.

rows.subject: DriveGPT
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation cross-entropy against number of unique training samples across model-size curves.

conditions.value: all data points except the 1.5M curve

rows.note: The authors describe the fit as exponential in the plotted quantities and say data-scaling results are relatively consistent across model sizes. This is a driving behavior model, not a language model.
rows.check: Drop V7: the fit compares no fitting choices. The 'exponential' fit is linear in log-log, i.e. a power law L∝D^-0.102, over 2.2M–120M samples (about 1.7 orders of magnitude). The 1.5M-parameter curve is excluded from the fit.

rows.subject: DriveGPT
rows.operation_detail: Vary model size and measure validation loss at different training-data sizes.
rows.value: The impact of larger models on validation loss is described as barely noticeable across a large range of model sizes.
rows.note: The result is stated for datasets up to 21M samples; the figure does not provide numerical loss values in the text.
rows.check: Drop V7. Flat model-size scaling at ≤21M samples is a data bottleneck, which standard L(N,D) expects, not evidence of fit-dependence. It means the model-size power law is not tested here with data non-limiting.

rows.subject: DriveGPT
rows.operation_detail: Vary model size and measure validation loss at different training-data sizes.
rows.value: Validation loss improves with larger models up to 12M parameters.
rows.note: The text does not give the numerical loss values.
rows.check: Drop V7. Loss gains stop at 12M parameters with 42M samples, consistent with a data bottleneck. No numbers are given.

rows.subject: DriveGPT
rows.operation_detail: Vary model size and measure validation loss at different training-data sizes.
rows.value: Validation loss improves with larger models up to 94M parameters; the authors describe diminishing returns beyond 94M.
rows.note: The text does not give numerical loss values; the stated plateau/diminishing-return behavior qualifies a single continuing power-law trend.
rows.check: Drop V7. Gains continue up to 94M parameters, then plateau and eventually overfit at 120M samples. No model-size exponent is fitted.

rows.subject: DriveGPT
rows.operation_detail: Measure training loss as a function of compute measured in FLOPs.
rows.value: Training loss generally decreases as compute increases; the decrease is initially steep and gradually slows at higher FLOPs. The paper also reports a plateau and eventual overfitting in its model-scaling discussion.
rows.note: The text says this compute range covers only a subset of the full range explored in the cited language-model studies. No fitted compute-loss exponent is reported.
rows.check: Drop V7. The measure is smoothed training loss, not held-out loss, and no compute exponent is fitted. The FLOP range covers only a subset of the LLM studies' range.

rows.subject: DriveGPT
rows.operation_detail: Compare model-size and data allocations within fixed compute-budget groups, keeping the product of resources constant.
rows.measure: Performance (the scaling experiment's loss/performance measure) and selected model size
rows.value: Larger compute budgets lead to better performance and an increasing optimal model size; the smallest model outperforms others in the three largest FLOP groups.
rows.note: The paper does not report an allocation exponent or numerical parameter/data splits for each budget; it interprets the result as evidence that data is the main bottleneck.
rows.check: Optimal model size rises with compute, yet the smallest model is best in the three largest FLOP groups. No allocation exponent or token/parameter splits are reported.

source_check.correct: State: cannot_determine for V3's stable allocation powers. Optimal model size increases with compute; the smallest tested model wins in the three largest FLOP groups. No allocation exponent is reported.
source_check.problem: An increasing selected model size does not establish partial adherence to a stable power law; boundary optima leave the allocation law undetermined.

rows.subject: DriveGPT
rows.size_stated: hidden dimensions specified in Table 2; exact sizes vary by configuration
rows.operation_detail: Vary attention-head configurations while keeping hidden dimension fixed.
rows.value: More decoder attention heads tend to improve performance for small models; overall scaling trend is more influenced by hidden dimension than by head count when hidden dimension is fixed.
rows.note: The paper says some configurations were omitted for the last group because of memory constraints. The text does not supply numerical loss values.
rows.check: Head count is varied at fixed hidden dimension, so parameter count is roughly fixed. Section 4.2 says this causes no noticeable change in results. A small-model decoder-head effect is noted.

rows.subject: DriveGPT
rows.operation_detail: Scale only the autoregressive decoder or only the encoder, compared with scaling both.
rows.value: Decoder-only scaling has a similar trend but worse performance, especially above 10M parameters on the two larger datasets.
rows.note: No numerical loss values are stated.
rows.check: This compares how parameters are split between encoder and decoder at a given total. Decoder-only scaling is worse above 10M parameters; the size of the gap is not given.

rows.subject: DriveGPT
rows.operation_detail: Scale only the encoder, compared with scaling both encoder and decoder.
rows.value: Encoder scaling is not as effective; scaling only the encoder has little impact beyond 10M parameters.
rows.note: No numerical loss values are stated.
rows.check: Encoder-only scaling gives little benefit beyond 10M parameters. The magnitude is not stated.

rows.subject: DriveGPT autoregressive decoder and one-shot decoder
rows.size_stated: scaled over two orders of magnitude
rows.operation_detail: Compare scaling an autoregressive decoder with a one-shot decoder.
rows.value: The autoregressive decoder is worse at small scale but outperforms the one-shot baseline beyond 8M parameters.
rows.note: The authors use minFDE because the two architectures have different loss definitions. This is an architecture-performance comparison, not a held-out cross-entropy comparison.
rows.check: This compares architecture families (the authors' autoregressive decoder vs a one-shot decoder) on minFDE. It is neither a shape-within-a-range comparison at fixed parameters nor a loss measure.

rows.subject: DriveGPT
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate planning metrics for one model trained on datasets of different sizes.
rows.measure: Normalized planning metrics: minADE, minFDE, miss rate, offroad rate, and collision rate
rows.value: The paper states that more training data significantly improves predicted-trajectory quality across all reported metrics; Table 3 gives normalized values for each data size.
rows.note: The table extraction does not reliably preserve the mapping of its five metric columns to the displayed values, so no individual metric values are assigned here.
rows.check: From Table 3, the first column (mADE) is 1.000, 0.561, 0.496, 0.489 and collision is 1.000, 0.269, 0.217, 0.196. All metrics improve monotonically with data, with diminishing returns.

rows.subject: DriveGPT
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate planning metrics for models of different sizes, trained on 120M samples.
rows.measure: Normalized planning metrics: minADE, minFDE, miss rate, offroad rate, and collision rate
rows.value: The paper states that all metrics improve up to 94M parameters and collision rate continues to improve at 163M; Table 4 gives normalized values for each model size.
rows.note: The table extraction does not reliably preserve the mapping of its five metric columns to the displayed values. The text reports the different endpoint for collision rate.
rows.check: From Table 4, mADE is 1.000, 0.954, 0.937, 0.943, so it worsens slightly at 163M. Collision is 0.817 at 163M vs 0.890 at 94M, even though validation loss has plateaued beyond 94M.

rows.subject: DriveGPT-Finetune
rows.stage_stated: pretraining on internal data followed by fine-tuning on WOMD
rows.operation_detail: Increase the amount of internal pretraining data before fine-tuning on WOMD.
rows.measure: WOMD vehicle prediction minADE, minFDE, and miss rate, averaged over three horizons
rows.baseline: DriveGPT-WOMD without internal pretraining: minADE 0.6381, minFDE 1.2846, miss rate 0.1233
rows.note: The comparison is from the validation results; the improvement over the no-internal-pretraining baseline is small at this data size.

rows.stage_stated: pretraining on internal data followed by fine-tuning on WOMD

rows.measure: WOMD vehicle prediction minADE, minFDE, and miss rate, averaged over three horizons
rows.baseline: DriveGPT-WOMD without internal pretraining: minADE 0.6381, minFDE 1.2846, miss rate 0.1233

source_check.reason: No model-size or compute power-law fit is reported. Model saturation is explicitly attributed to limited data, an existing bottleneck qualification of the underlying scaling claim. Unfitted powers and a different loss measure do not themselves establish a scope limitation.
